content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed toolkits such as the MyopiaED and mSafeListening handbooks to assist policymakers and implementers in establishing large-scale national programs aimed at preventing myopia and hearing loss. These programs leverage smartphone technology platforms to enhance their reach and effectiveness. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries adopted remote services to deliver comprehensive sexuality education, demonstrating the potential for such services to remain valuable beyond the pandemic context. It is essential to conduct regular evaluations of services delivered through digital and mobile technologies before expanding them or replacing existing care models. Investing in activated adolescent patients is critical; this concept refers to equipping adolescents with the skills and confidence to actively engage in their healthcare. Programs should also focus on building self-care skills for pregnant adolescents and those living with HIV or other chronic conditions, ensuring coordination with existing services and fostering a supportive sociopolitical environment. Community health workers play a vital role in reaching adolescents, particularly those out of school, with health education and services. Governments should establish mechanisms to formally engage non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in service delivery to strengthen community-based platforms and reach underserved adolescent populations. For example, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the government is working to improve access to quality sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services for adolescents and youth. Despite adolescents comprising one-third of the population, only 17% accessed health services in 2021. To address this, WHO has supported a collaborative learning project to improve service quality, where providers work together to identify and solve common challenges, ultimately enhancing adolescent health services. Adolescents require tailored services, as emphasized by the Director of the National Programme of Adolescent Health in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Collaborative learning strengthens provider capacities and attitudes, leading to improved care. For instance, a nurse in Kinshasa reported a significant increase in adolescent attendance at her health center after participating in training sessions. Satisfaction rates among adolescents reached 100%, and the project is now scaling up to additional zones based on its initial success. School health services (SHS) are critical for promoting health and well-being among students, whether healthy or managing chronic conditions. Schools provide a unique platform to deliver health services due to their extensive contact with children and adolescents. SHS programs often include safe water and sanitation, health education, and nutrition services, tailored to local needs. Well-adolescent visits, which are system-supported or scheduled encounters between adolescents and healthcare providers, offer opportunities for holistic assessments, early interventions, and anticipatory guidance. These visits are less common for adolescents compared to younger children, but they hold significant potential for addressing physical, emotional, and psychosocial needs. Pre-visit psychosocial assessments, completed by adolescents before consultations, help identify underlying issues that may not be immediately apparent. These assessments improve early detection and timely intervention for health and well-being challenges, particularly during adolescence when psychosocial issues and risky behaviors are prevalent. Tools like the HEADSSS framework (covering home, education, activities, drugs, suicidality, sex, and safety) have proven effective in detecting health concerns and facilitating interventions. Digital versions of these tools further enhance accessibility and efficiency. National health information systems often lack ageand sex-disaggregated data specific to adolescents, particularly in countries with large adolescent populations and high disease burdens. Programs should prioritize collecting and analyzing such data to address health inequities and inform targeted interventions. Teleconsultations, which use information and communication technologies to provide remote health services, offer numerous benefits, including improved access to care, reduced infection risks, and enhanced flexibility for managing chronic conditions. The education sector plays a crucial role in adolescent health and well-being. Healthy, well-nourished, and happy students perform better academically and are more likely to lead fulfilling lives. Schools can promote health through initiatives such as healthy meals, inclusive environments, and linking students to healthcare services. WHO and UNESCO have developed global standards for health-promoting schools to help governments integrate health and nutrition into education systems. Strengthening intersectoral coordination, updating school health policies, and investing in school infrastructure are essential strategies for enhancing the education sector's role in adolescent health. In France, school health services are designed to make schools health-promoting environments. School doctors, who are attached to the Ministry of Education, undergo specialized training to shift their focus from curative to preventive care and from individual to collective perspectives. This training equips them with competencies specific to school health, enabling them to address health inequalities and promote well-being among students. The French system highlights the importance of preparing school doctors to adapt to evolving health and education needs, ensuring that schools adopt a comprehensive health promotion approach.
